correctness.rationale: Direct two-sample expectation yields s3(1+s2)-2s2² exactly. For m<=4, padding to four and Cauchy bound each mass by a=[1+sqrt(3(4s2-1))]/4. Summing (p_i-b)^2(p_i-a)<=0 proves sharp s3<=a³+3b³; resulting bound is 2(a-1)^3(16a²-2a+1)/27<0 for any nondegenerate law. Five-atom explicit masses give s2=13/20,s3=41/80,cov=1/1600. Uniform examples negative, and continuity on the open simplex gives zero and all larger positive examples. A stand-alone exact-rational direct enumeration independently passed 2,444 comparisons. Finite enumeration does not replace the analytic proof.

originality.rationale: The accepted scientific contribution is the first-support-five three-sign classification, not the standard Good–Turing estimator, elementary moment identity, or a generic risk estimator. Same-quantity primary comparisons covered Skorski 2021 exact problem set and Theorems 1–3 on worst MSE; Cohen–Routtenberg–Tong 2021/2022 miss-mass estimation bounds; Painsky 2021/2023 abstract on generalized risk; and published-finding corpus published findings on missing-mass successive discoveries and covariance of other occupancy diagnostics. Neither inspected primary text nor checked record summary gives the exact cutoff for sign of Cov(U,N_1/2) at n=2. General risk formulas may furnish algebraic component moments, but their reported maximization objective differs and does not establish the sharp four-coordinate inequality. Painsky full text inaccessible, so a residual priority risk is stated.
residual_risks: Painsky full paper/supplement not inspected: a covariance or exact risk decomposition may cover part of the result.

value.rationale: A natural support-size threshold governs whether the classical Good–Turing unseen-mass estimator is positively associated with its *realized* target after the smallest informative sample. This is a complete all-laws sign classification for fixed sample size two, with a sharp four-support inequality, exact minimal five-support witness, and connectedness proof for all three signs. No unsupported claims about estimator risk, practical performance, or larger sample sizes.
